{{short description|Array of partial sums of the binomial coefficients}}
[[File:Bernoulli triangle derivation.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Derivation of Bernoulli's triangle (blue bold text) from Pascal's triangle (pink italics)]]
'''Bernoulli's triangle''' is an [[Matrix (mathematics)|array]] of [[partial sums]] of the [[binomial coefficients]]. For any non-negative integer ''n'' and for any integer ''k'' included between 0 and ''n'', the component in row ''n'' and column ''k'' is given by:

:<math> \sum_{p=0}^k {n \choose p}, </math>

[[File:pascal triangle compositions.svg|thumb|As the numbers of [[composition (combinatorics)|com&shy;po&shy;si&shy;tions]] of ''n''+1 into ''k''+1 ordered partitions form [[Pascal's triangle]], the numbers of [[composition (combinatorics)|compositions]] of ''n''+1 into ''k''+1 '''''or fewer''''' ordered partitions form Bernoulli's triangle]]

i.e., the sum of the first ''k'' ''n''th-order binomial coefficients.<ref>[http://oeis.org/wiki/Bernoulli%27s_triangle On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]</ref> The first rows of Bernoulli's triangle are:

: <math>
\begin{array}{cc|cccccc}
& k & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5\\
n & & \\
\hline
0 & & 1 \\
1 & & 1 & 2 \\
2 & & 1 & 3 & 4 \\
3 & & 1 & 4 & 7 & 8 \\
4 & & 1 & 5 & 11 & 15 & 16 \\
5 & & 1 & 6 & 16 & 26 & 31 & 32
\end{array}
</math>

Similarly to [[Pascal's triangle]], each component of Bernoulli's triangle is the sum of two components of the previous row, except for the last number of each row, which is double the last number of the previous row.  For example, if <math>B_{n,k}</math> denotes the component in row ''n'' and column ''k'', then:

:<math>
B_{n,k}=\begin{cases}
                    1 & \mbox{if  } n=0 \\
B_{n-1,k}+B_{n-1,k-1} & \mbox{if  } k<n \\
   2B_{n-1,k-1} = 2^n & \mbox{if  } k=n
\end{cases}
</math>

==Sequences derived from Bernoulli's triangle==

[[File:Bernoulli triangle columns.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Sequences from the [[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]] in Bernoulli's triangle]]
As in Pascal's triangle and other similarly constructed triangles,<ref>Hoggatt, Jr, V. E., A new angle on Pascal's triangle, ''Fibonacci Quarterly'' '''6'''(4) (1968) 221–234; Hoggatt, Jr, V. E., Convolution triangles for generalized Fibonacci numbers, ''Fibonacci Quarterly'' '''8'''(2) (1970) 158–171</ref> sums of components along diagonal paths in Bernoulli's triangle result in the [[Fibonacci number]]s.<ref>Neiter, D. & Proag, A., [https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL19/Proag/proag3.html Links Between Sums Over Paths in Bernoulli's Triangles and the Fibonacci Numbers], ''Journal of Integer Sequences'', '''19''' (2016) 16.8.3.</ref>

As the third column of Bernoulli's triangle (''k'' = 2) is a triangular number plus one, it forms the [[lazy caterer's sequence]] for ''n'' cuts, where ''n'' &ge; 2.<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A000124|Central polygonal numbers (the Lazy Caterer's sequence)}}</ref> The fourth column (''k'' = 3) is the three-dimensional analogue, known as the [[cake number]]s, for ''n'' cuts, where ''n'' &ge; 3.<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A000125|Cake numbers}}</ref>

The fifth column (''k'' = 4) gives the maximum number of regions in the problem of [[dividing a circle into areas]] for ''n'' + 1 points, where ''n'' &ge; 4.<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A000127}}</ref>

In general, the (''k'' + 1)th column gives the maximum number of regions in [[space (mathematics)|''k''-dimensional space]] formed by {{nowrap|''n'' &minus; 1}} {{nowrap|(''k'' &minus; 1)-dimensional}} [[hyperplane]]s, for ''n'' &ge; ''k''.<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A006261}}</ref> It also gives the number of [[composition (combinatorics)|compositions]] (ordered partitions) of ''n'' + 1 into ''k'' + 1 or fewer parts.<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A008861}}</ref>
